questions.text: What is the main challenge with phrasal verbs according to the text?
opts: You cannot predict their meaning from individual words
Native speakers use them too fast
questions.correct: You cannot predict their meaning from individual words
questions.hint: "The meaning is idiomatic — the combination creates something new."

questions.text: What approach does Rustam recommend for learning phrasal verbs?
questions.hint: "I started learning them in context — in sentences, in dialogues, in things people actually said."

questions.text: Phrasal verbs are always informal in English.
questions.hint: "Many are used in business, academic, and professional contexts: 'carry out research'..."

questions.text: What does the particle "out" often suggest?
questions.hint: "'Out' often suggests completion or emergence: 'sort out', 'find out', 'work out'."

questions.text: What is Amir's strategy?
opts: Hear phrasal verbs in songs/films and try to guess first
questions.correct: Hear phrasal verbs in songs/films and try to guess first
questions.hint: "I learn phrasal verbs through songs and films... I try to guess first. Then I check."

questions.text: What makes English prose sound "bookish"?
opts: Using only single-word verbs instead of natural phrasal verbs
questions.correct: Using only single-word verbs instead of natural phrasal verbs
questions.hint: "If you use single-word verbs in casual conversation, you may sound slightly formal or bookish."

questions.text: Why is Zhibek struggling?
opts: The research is taking up too much time alongside volleyball and coursework
She had a fight with the professor
questions.correct: The research is taking up too much time alongside volleyball and coursework
questions.hint: "It's taking up too much time. I can't keep up with my coursework and volleyball training."

questions.text: What does "putting it off" mean in the conversation?
questions.hint: "I keep putting it off." = keep postponing/delaying the meeting.

questions.text: What does Amir advise Zhibek to do?
opts: Bring up the issue with Sultanova and sort it out
Ask for more time at the end of semester
questions.correct: Bring up the issue with Sultanova and sort it out
questions.hint: "You should bring it up soon... carry on like this without saying anything, you'll burn out."

questions.text: Zhibek says she doesn't want to ___ her professor.
questions.hint: "I don't want to let her down." = disappoint Professor Sultanova.

questions.text: What does Zhibek decide at the end?
opts: Set up a meeting with Sultanova tomorrow
questions.correct: Set up a meeting with Sultanova tomorrow
questions.hint: "I'll set up a meeting with her tomorrow."

questions.text: What does Amir offer to do?
opts: Go over what she should say together
questions.correct: Go over what she should say together
questions.hint: "Write down the main points first. Then we'll go over it together."

questions.text: "Turn off the light." With pronoun becomes:
questions.hint: Separable: pronoun goes INSIDE. "Turn IT off." ✅

questions.text: "Look after him." — Is "look him after" correct?
questions.hint: "look after" = inseparable. Object ALWAYS after: "Look after HIM." ✅ Never "look him after."

questions.text: "I sorted out the problem." → "I sorted ___ ."
questions.hint: Separable: pronoun inside. "I sorted IT OUT." ✅

questions.text: "I ran into him." — This is correct because:
opts: Pronouns always go after the particle in separable verbs
"run into" is inseparable — object always after
questions.correct: "run into" is inseparable — object always after
questions.hint: "run into" = inseparable. Object after: "ran INTO him." ✅

questions.text: "Set ___ it" — Choose correctly.
questions.hint: Separable: "Set UP IT" would place pronoun at the end → wrong! With pronoun: "Set IT up." But "set up it" = wrong order. "Set it up." ✅

questions.text: "Put up with" is a ___ phrasal verb.
questions.hint: "put up with" = 3-part inseparable. Object always after "with": "put up WITH it." ✅

questions.text: "She came ___ a great article." (find by chance)
questions.hint: "come across" = find by chance. Inseparable. "She came ACROSS a great article." ✅

questions.text: "Find out the answer." With pronoun:
questions.hint: Separable: pronoun inside. "Find IT out." ✅ NOT "find out it."

questions.text: "Put up with" means:
questions.hint: "put up with" = to tolerate; to accept something unpleasant without complaining.

questions.text: "Give up" means:
questions.hint: "give up" = to stop trying to do something; to abandon a plan or activity.

questions.text: She ___ (searched for) the word in the dictionary.
questions.hint: "look up" = to search for information in a reference. "She LOOKED UP the word." ✅

questions.text: "Carry on" means:
questions.hint: "carry on" = to continue doing something, often despite difficulties.

questions.text: "Come across" can mean:
opts: To find something by chance OR to seem/appear a certain way
questions.correct: To find something by chance OR to seem/appear a certain way
questions.hint: "come across" = 1) to find by chance ("I came across an interesting article.") 2) to seem ("She comes across as very confident.")
